summary: Defines the Host-bit (H-bit) for OSPFv2, which lets a router advertise that it is a non-transit router so other routers will not send transit traffic through it. It also describes the changes needed to support the bit and updates RFC 6987.

eli5.summary: A dead-end street sign that tells drivers not to use it as a shortcut, because it only serves the houses on it.

questions: how can an ospf router avoid transit traffic
how does ospf avoid transit traffic
what is ospf host router capability
how does ospf graceful isolation work
subtitle: A single bit that lets an OSPFv2 router say: send traffic to me, never through me.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 has no way for a router to refuse transit traffic when it sits on the only or shortest path. Raising its metrics only helps if a better alternative route exists.
tldr.mechanism: A new Host-bit (H-bit) in the router-LSA marks a router as non-transit, and the SPF calculation skips such routers as transit vertices. A Router Information capability bit checks that every router in the area understands this, and Type 2 external metrics are raised to LSInfinity-1 or LSInfinity.
tldr.outcome: A router can be isolated gracefully or kept out of the forwarding path while still being reachable for its own local destinations. The RFC updates RFC 6987 and is itself updated by a later RFC.

today: RFC 8770 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6987. It has itself been updated by RFC 10041.

sections.title: Why Transit Traffic Needs Repelling
sections.content:
OSPFv2 runs a Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm that finds transit vertices from their adjacencies. It therefore has no way to keep traffic from passing through a router that is the only path, or the shortest path, to a destination. Making the router's metrics bad helps only if a better route exists.

The RFC lists four uses for a mechanism that moves traffic away: graceful isolation of a router before a reload to avoid blackholes, closet switches that must join the topology but are not meant for transit, overloaded routers that want to shed traffic until they stabilize, and BGP route reflectors in places such as data centers that learn the OSPF topology but cannot forward transit traffic.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a road should not be used as a shortcut, like a quiet street full of homes. Making it look worse only works if another road exists, so the street needs a proper "no through traffic" sign.

sections.title: The Host-Bit
sections.content:
RFC 8770 defines a new router-LSA bit, the Host-bit or H-bit. It is the high-order bit of the router-LSA flags byte, next to the existing N, W, V, E and B bits. A router that sets it tells the other OSPFv2 routers in the area that support the feature that it MUST NOT be used as a transit router. Other routers may still send traffic to its local destinations. If the bit is not set, behavior is the same as in RFC 2328.

A router that originates a router-LSA with the H-bit set MUST advertise all its non-stub links with a cost of MaxLinkMetric, as defined in RFC 6987.

An Area Border Router (ABR) with the H-bit set MUST advertise the same setting in its router-LSAs for all attached areas. It then advertises only IPv4 prefixes tied to its local interfaces in summary-LSAs. A host router cannot act as an ASBR: non-local prefixes, such as those imported from other protocols, SHOULD NOT be advertised in AS-external-LSAs.
sections.eli5: A router puts up a flag that says "I am a host, not a road". It also makes its own roads look terribly expensive, so nobody picks them by mistake.

sections.title: The SPF Change
sections.content:
The SPF calculation in Section 16.1 of RFC 2328 gets one extra check in step (2). When the vertex just added to the tree is a router-LSA with the H-bit set, and the vertex is not the root, the router is not used for transit and the calculation moves straight to step (3).

The root exception matters: a router with the H-bit set still computes routes from its own point of view. All other sub-procedures of step (2) stay unchanged.
sections.eli5: When the map-maker finds a street marked "houses only", they draw the houses but do not plan any route that goes through it.

sections.title: Autodiscovery and Partial Deployment
sections.content:
If only some routers understand the H-bit, routing loops could form. To avoid this, the RFC defines an OSPF Router Information (RI) LSA capability bit, the OSPF Host Router capability, from RFC 7770. The RI LSA MUST be area-scoped.

Routers that support the H-bit MUST check the RI LSAs of all nodes in the area before using the feature. If any router does not advertise the capability, the SPF modifications MUST NOT be used in that area. All routers with the H-bit set MUST also advertise their non-stub links with MaxLinkMetric, so routers without H-bit support avoid them unless they are the last resort.

Implementations are RECOMMENDED to offer a configuration parameter to override enforcement in partial deployments where the topology guarantees that routers lacking H-bit support cannot cause loops. Temporary transient loops are still possible while the RI LSA of a newly joined router propagates.
sections.eli5: The "houses only" sign only works if every driver can read it. So the routers first check that everybody in the neighborhood knows what it means.

sections.title: Type 2 External Metrics
sections.content:
For AS-external-LSAs and NSSA-LSAs with a Type 2 metric, the advertised Type 2 metric counts for more than the OSPF intra-area or inter-area path. So advertising links with MaxLinkMetric does not discourage transit traffic toward such routes.

RFC 8770 therefore updates RFC 6987: the Type 2 metric in any self-originated AS-external-LSA or NSSA-LSA is advertised as LSInfinity-1. If the H-bit is set, the Type 2 metric MUST be set to LSInfinity.
sections.eli5: For some far-away destinations, the price tag on the last leg counts more than the price of the road. So the router also puts a sky-high price on that part.

sections.title: Security and Rogue Routers
sections.content:
The H-bit only restricts a router to a subset of normal router operation, so the RFC says it should not add security considerations beyond those of RFC 2328. The RFC walks through three cases of a rogue or buggy router.

  • It lacks the capability but sets the H-bit: a loop is possible, but the MaxLinkMetric cost makes the router avoided anyway.
  • It has the capability but leaves the H-bit clear: it stops other routers from running the modified SPF, though the others still advertise MaxLinkMetric.
  • It sits on the only transit path and sets the H-bit: this can partition the network, and cannot be told apart from an operator doing maintenance on purpose. OSPF keeps working inside the partitions.
sections.eli5: If someone puts up a fake sign, the worst case is some roads get avoided. The expensive-road trick limits the damage.
